Parity ∉𝖰𝖠𝖢0\notin\mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0} ⇔\iff 𝖰𝖠𝖢0\mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0} is Fourier-Concentrated

Lucas Gretta ††thanks: University of California at Berkeley. Email: lucas_gretta@berkeley.edu. Supported by NSF Award CCF-2231095.    Meghal Gupta ††thanks: University of California at Berkeley. Email: meghal@berkeley.edu. Supported by NSF GRFP.    Malvika Raj Joshi ††thanks: University of California at Berkeley. Email: malvika@berkeley.edu. Supported by NSF grant 2311733 and DOE grant DE-SC0024124.
Abstract

A major open problem in understanding shallow quantum circuits (𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}) is whether they can compute PARITY. In this work, we show that this question is solely about the Fourier spectrum of 𝖰𝖠𝖢0\mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0}: any 𝖰𝖠𝖢0\mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0} circuit with non-negligible high-level Fourier mass suffices to exactly compute PARITY in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. Thus, proving a quantum analog of the seminal LMN theorem for 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} [22] is necessary to bound the quantum circuit complexity of PARITY.

In the other direction, LMN does not fully capture the limitations of 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0}. For example, despite MAJORITY having 99%99\% of its weight on low-degree Fourier coefficients, no 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} circuit can non-trivially correlate with it [26, 28]. In contrast, we provide a 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit that achieves (1−o⁡(1))(1-o(1)) correlation with MAJORITY, establishing the first average-case decision separation between 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} and 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. This suggests a uniquely quantum phenomenon: unlike in the classical setting, Fourier concentration may largely characterize the power of 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}.

PARITY is also known to be equivalent in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} to inherently quantum tasks such as preparing GHZ states to high fidelity. We extend this equivalence to a broad class of state-synthesis tasks. We demonstrate that existing measures such as trace distance, fidelity, and mutual information are insufficient to capture these states and introduce a new measure, felinity. We prove that preparing any state with non-negligible felinity, or derived states such as 𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n){\mathsf{poly}}(n)-weight Dicke states, implies PARITY∈𝖰𝖠𝖢0\texttt{PARITY}\in\mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0}.

1 Introduction

Understanding the computational power of constant-depth quantum circuits (𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}) remains a central open problem in quantum complexity theory.

Classical constant-depth circuits (𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0}) cannot compute PARITY [3, 10, 17] and in fact, form a strict hierarchy. Adding PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n} gates to 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} does not enable other hard computations such as arbitrary modular arithmetic or MAJORITYn\texttt{MAJORITY}_{n}, making 𝖠𝖢0⊊𝖠𝖢0​[2]⊊𝖠𝖢𝖢⊆𝖳𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0}\subsetneq{\mathsf{AC}}^{0}[2]\subsetneq{\mathsf{ACC}}\subseteq{\mathsf{TC}}^{0} [26, 28]. In contrast, 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} exhibits an “all-or-nothing” behavior [29]. The class 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}, obtained by augmenting 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} with PARITY gates (or its Hadamard conjugate FANOUT), can simulate all of 𝖳𝖢0{\mathsf{TC}}^{0} [23, 19]. Thus, determining whether 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} can compute PARITY, or equivalently, whether 𝖰𝖠𝖢0=𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}={\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}, is a crucial step.

A distinctive feature of PARITY is that all of its Fourier mass lies on the highest-degree coefficient. However, 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} circuits exhibit strong concentration on low-degree Fourier coefficients, a landmark result known eponymously by LMN [22]. Subsequent works have led to a tight characterization of this Fourier spectrum [16, 30]. This suggests a natural approach to resolving whether PARITY∈𝖰𝖠𝖢0\texttt{PARITY}\in{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} by seeking an analogous characterization for 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. The Fourier spectrum of 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuits, induced by measuring the output qubit, has been conjectured to exhibit low degree concentration [24, 4], suggesting a quantum analog of LMN (“QLMN”) may hold. Informally, this conjecture states that the 𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n){\mathsf{poly}}(n)-level Fourier coefficients have negligible (n−ω⁡(1)n^{-\omega(1)}) weight. A fully parameterized version of this conjecture, analogous to the true LMN is stated in Conjecture 1.

Clearly, if the QLMN conjecture were true, then PARITY∉𝖰𝖠𝖢0\texttt{PARITY}\not\in{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. In this work, we show that the reverse implication also holds:

PARITY∉𝖰𝖠𝖢0⟺QLMN.\texttt{PARITY}\not\in{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}\Longleftrightarrow\mathrm{QLMN}.

In other words, proving QLMN is necessary for proving PARITY∉𝖰𝖠𝖢0\texttt{PARITY}\not\in{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}.

Another interpretation of our result is that any single-output 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit with non-negligible high-level Fourier mass (Definition 3.1) suffices to compute PARITY in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. This equivalence has no classical analog because adding a gate to 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} that only approximates some arbitrary high-degree boolean function, does not necessarily produce 𝖠𝖢0​[2]{\mathsf{AC}}^{0}[2].

An immediate consequence of our result is that any 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit achieving non-negligible correlation with PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n} on a random input provides a 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit for computing PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n} exactly. Similarly, it suffices to construct a circuit with 1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1-1/{\mathsf{poly}}(n) correlation with MAJORITYn\texttt{MAJORITY}_{n} on average, or a circuit with 1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1/{\mathsf{poly}}(n) advantage for MAJORITY in the worst case to obtain exact PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n}. These results and others are summarized in Table 1 below. Prior work of [13] introduced the worst-case bounded error classes 𝖡𝖰𝖠𝖢0\mathsf{BQAC}^{0}, 𝖡𝖰𝖳𝖢0\mathsf{BQTC}^{0}, and [12] subsequently showed 𝖡𝖰𝖳𝖢0=𝖡𝖰𝖠𝖢f0\mathsf{BQTC}^{0}=\mathsf{BQAC}^{0}_{f} and QTC0=𝖰𝖠𝖢f0\textsf{QTC}^{0}={\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}. In regards to these classes, our results imply that if MAJORITY∈𝖡𝖰𝖠𝖢0\texttt{MAJORITY}\in\mathsf{BQAC}^{0}, then 𝖰𝖠𝖢0=𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}={\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}.

An average-case separation.

MAJORITY is often used to illustrate limitations of Fourier-concentration for obtaining average-case 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} lower bounds. Despite the Majority function having 1−o⁡(1)1-o(1) of its weight on low-degree Fourier coefficients, 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} circuits cannot achieve better than Θ⁡(1n)\Theta\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\right)-correlation with MAJORITY [26, 28]. We, however, show that a 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit can achieve (1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n))(1-1/{\mathsf{polylog}}(n)) correlation with MAJORITYn\texttt{MAJORITY}_{n}. This establishes the first average-case decision problem separation between 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} and 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. Furthermore, this sharp contrast with the classical setting suggests that, in the quantum world, Fourier concentration may be largely sufficient to characterize 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. Indeed, by combining this result with our aforementioned hardness result, we see that the feasible regimes of MAJORITY in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} are essentially determined by QLMN.

Consequences for hardness of state synthesis.

It is well-known that preparing the cat state (12​|0n⟩+12​|1n⟩\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{0^{n}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{1^{n}}) or a nekomata state (|0n⟩​⟨0n|+|1n⟩​⟨1n|)(\outerproduct*{0^n}{0^n}+\outerproduct*{1^n}{1^n}) in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} is equivalent to computing PARITY in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. This equivalence also holds for preparing high-fidelity (i.e. 1−ε1-\varepsilon) approximations to these states [23, 27, 12]. However, we show that there are much weaker approximations whose preparation implies PARITY∈𝖰𝖠𝖢0\texttt{PARITY}\in{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, but these cannot be distinguished from states known to be in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} through existing measures. To more extensively capture state synthesis tasks that are as hard as PARITY, we introduce a new notion, felinity (Definition 2.1). The felinity of a nn-qubit state ρ\rho directly quantifies the ability of a circuit for ρ\rho to correlate with PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n}. Combined with our main result, this yields a large class of states whose preparation as black-box immediately unlock the full power of 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}.

Another family of quantum states of interest is Dicke states, defined as uniform superpositions over nn-bit strings of Hamming weight kk (WLOG k≤n/2k\leq n/2). Recent work shows that FANOUTn\texttt{FANOUT}_{n} enables preparation of arbitrary-weight states in 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f} [21]. However, it was previously unknown whether this reliance on fanout is necessary. Using felinity, we show that FANOUTk\texttt{FANOUT}_{k} is necessary to prepare Dicke states of weight kk. Consequently, for any k=𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)k={\mathsf{poly}}(n), such as k=n0.0001k=n^{0.0001}, the ability to prepare weight-kk Dicke states in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} would imply 𝖰𝖠𝖢0=𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}={\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}.

1.1 Our results

We show that the Fourier concentration of 𝖰𝖠𝖢{\mathsf{QAC}} functions is intimately related to the hardness of PARITY in 𝖰𝖠𝖢{\mathsf{QAC}}. More formally, define 𝖰𝖠𝖢⁡(d,s){\mathsf{QAC}}(d,s) to be 𝖰𝖠𝖢{\mathsf{QAC}} circuits with depth ≤d\leq d and size ≤s\leq s11 1 There is some subtlety based on whether 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} is defined to have polynomial ancillae or polynomial gates. In this paper this concern is largely not important, as our reductions achieve proportional blowup in both measures. and define the QLMN​(γ​(d,k))\text{QLMN}(\gamma(d,k)) to be the following proposition, parameterized based on a decay function γ:ℕ×ℕ→ℕ\gamma:\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}, similar to the way the classical [22] is parameterized.

𝐖≥k​[f𝒞]<s⋅γ​(d,k)−1.\mathbf{W}^{\geq k}\left[f_{\mathcal{C}}\right]<s\cdot\gamma(d,k)^{-1}.

Note that setting γ⁡(d,k):=2Ω⁡(k1/d)\gamma(d,k):=2^{\Omega\left(k^{1/d}\right)} would conjecture the analog of classical LMN. We show that proving strong lower bounds on the size/depth complexity of PARITY in 𝖰𝖠𝖢{\mathsf{QAC}} necessitates proving QLMN under corresponding parameters.

Theorem 1.1 (Equivalence of QLMN and Hardness of Parity).

For all γ:ℕ×ℕ→ℕ\gamma:\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N},

QLMN⁡(γ)⇔PARITYn∉𝖰𝖠𝖢⁡(Θ⁡(d),Θ~​(γ⁡(d,n))).\mathrm{QLMN}(\gamma)\iff\texttt{PARITY}_{n}\not\in{\mathsf{QAC}}(\Theta(d),\widetilde{\Theta}(\gamma(d,n))).

Equivalently, letting S⁡(d,n)S(d,n) denote the maximum size such that no depth dd circuit of this size can compute PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n}, then QLMN​(Θ~​(S​(Θ​(d),k)))\text{QLMN}(\tilde{\Theta}\left(S(\Theta(d),k))\right) holds.

Here Θ\Theta hides absolute constants, and Θ~\tilde{\Theta} hides absolute constants and log factors. Note that the dependence on circuit size on the LHS is baked into the QLMN definition. Restricting to the case of 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, we have the following corollary.

Corollary 1.2.

QLMN​(𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒d​(kω⁡(1)))\text{QLMN}({\mathsf{poly}}_{d}(k^{\omega(1)})) holds for some 𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒d​(kω⁡(1)){\mathsf{poly}}_{d}(k^{\omega(1)}) if and only if PARITY∉𝖰𝖠𝖢0\texttt{PARITY}\notin{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}.

Next, we provide that a variety of approximation problems and state construction tasks that are 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete, or equivalently QTC0\textsf{QTC}^{0}-complete, under 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} reductions. Augmenting 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} gates with a “noisy” gate (and its inverse) for any one of the following tasks, provides the ability to implement any problem in 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f} without error.

Theorem 1.3 (𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete problems).

The following tasks are equivalent to exact FANOUTn under 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} reductions.

  1. 1.

    Any non-negligible PARITYn correlation (Section 2.1.1). Achieving non-negligible (i.e. ≥1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)\geq 1/{\mathsf{poly}}(n)) correlation with PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n} on a random input.

  2. 2.

    Weak nekomata-like states (Section 2.2). For any non-negl ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0, synthesizing a state ρ\rho satisfying ⟨0n|ρ|0n⟩≥ε,⟨1n|ρ|1n⟩≥ε\braket{0^{n}|\rho|0^{n}}\geq\varepsilon,\braket{1^{n}|\rho|1^{n}}\geq\varepsilon.

  3. 3.

    Poly-weight Dicke states (Section 2.2.1). For any δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) and k=Ω⁡(nδ)≤n/2k=\Omega(n^{\delta})\leq n/2, synthesizing a state with at least (1−ε)(1-\varepsilon) fidelity with |Dkn⟩\ket{D^{n}_{k}}.

  4. 4.

    High average case MAJORITYn correlation (Section 2.3). For any arbitrarily small constant δ>0\delta>0, achieving at least (1−1/nδ)(1-1/n^{\delta}) correlation with MAJORITYn\texttt{MAJORITY}_{n} on a random input.

  5. 5.

    Bounded worst case MAJORITYn error (Section 2.3). For any ε=1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n)\varepsilon=1/{\mathsf{polylog}}(n), achieving ε\varepsilon-correlation with MAJORITYn​(𝒙)\texttt{MAJORITY}_{n}({\bm{x}}) (correct wp ≥1/2+ε/2\geq 1/2+\varepsilon/2) on every input 𝒙∈{0,1}n{\bm{x}}\in\{0,1\}^{n}.

In other words, a 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit CC, whose m=𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)m={\mathsf{poly}}(n) ancillae start in |0m⟩\ket{0^{m}}, for any one of the above tasks implies 𝖰𝖠𝖢0=𝖰𝖠𝖢f0\mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0}=\mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0}_{f}.

Notice that “weak-nekomata-like states” can have much lower fidelity and trace-distance to any nekomata compared to states trivially in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, such as |0n⟩\ket{0^{n}}. Moreover for small enough ε0,ε1\varepsilon_{0},\varepsilon_{1}, they have much lower mutual information between qubits than the |Wn⟩\ket{W_{n}} state (weight 11 Dicke state), which can be synthesized exactly in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} [12, 21]. To reliably discern these hard states, we introduce a new measure, felinity (Section 4.2), and show that preparing any state with non-negligible felinity implies 𝖰𝖠𝖢0=𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}={\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f} (Section 2.2).

Finally, we crucially distinguish between average and worst case regimes for MAJORITY. This is in contrast to PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n}, where average case and worst case error regimes for PARITY are equivalent for 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} as well as 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} (with randomness). Both 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} and 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} can achieve Θ⁡(1/n)\Theta(1/\sqrt{n})-correlation with MAJORITY, i.e., 1/2+Θ⁡(1/n)1/2+\Theta(1/\sqrt{n}) success probability, on a random input by outputting the first input bit. It is also known that 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} cannot achieve better correlation than this for MAJORITY. However, our next result shows that this is not true for 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, thus establishing an average-case separation between the two classes.

Theorem 1.4 (Section 2.3.1 informal).

There exists a 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit that achieves any (1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n))(1-1/{\mathsf{polylog}}(n)) correlation with MAJORITY.

This brings us back to Moore’s original question of whether PARITYn∈{}_{n}\in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. This question is indeed the key to determining the computational power of 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, regardless of which notion of computation, exact/clean/approximate/average case/worst case, is used. Our results clear the path towards understanding 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} and motivate further study into the Fourier spectrum of 𝖰𝖠𝖢0\mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0}. From a practical standpoint, it is sufficient to produce a gate for one of the much weaker approximation tasks from Theorem 1.3 to unlock the full power of 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}, which includes modular arithmetic, QFT, sorting, and arbitrary Dicke state preparation [23, 11, 19, 29, 21].

1.2 Prior work

A key distinction between 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} and 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} circuits, arising from reversibility, is the role of FANOUT. In 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0}, copying the outputs of gates is free. Quantumly, due to the no-cloning theorem, copying the output of gates is impossible. Instead, FANOUT refers to copying the classical information of a qubit. The reversible FANOUTn\texttt{FANOUT}_{n} gate copies a qubit onto nn targets via XOR, and under Hadamard conjugation corresponds to a clean PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n} gate. Foundational work by [23] established equivalences between FANOUTn\texttt{FANOUT}_{n}, PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n}, and cat/GHZ states (|  n⟩=12​|0n⟩+12​|1n⟩)(\ket{\hbox{\hbox to8.18pt{\vbox \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}_{n}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{0^{n}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{1^{n}}). These can be thought of as complete problems under 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} reductions for the class obtained by including fan-out, 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}. Early works also showed that 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f} can implement arbitrary threshold functions, modular arithmetic, and more [23, 11, 19]. Subsequently, [27] discovered that preparing a “nekomata”, a weaker form of |n⟩\ket{{}_{n}} consisting of a mixture rather than a superposition, is also 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete. They leveraged this new reduction to provide the first constant depth approximation of PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n} using exponential size. This allowed for approximate-FANOUT𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n)\texttt{FANOUT}_{{\mathsf{polylog}}(n)} in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, which is limited to 𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n){\mathsf{poly}}(n) size. Thereafter, [13] showed that threshold gates also provide the ability to create approximate nekomata. Recently both constructions were made exact by [12], implying that QTC0=𝖰𝖠𝖢f0\textsf{QTC}^{0}={\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f} and FANOUT𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n)\texttt{FANOUT}_{{\mathsf{polylog}}(n)} can be exactly implemented in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. Existing prior work on upper bounds and reductions is summarized in Table 1.

Prior work such as [13, 27] has focused mainly on worst-case error regimes, where performance is measured by the error guarantee for all inputs. [27] showed reductions between the worst-case approximations of 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete problems. For high accuracy, such as (1−o⁡(1))(1-o(1)) fidelity with a nekomata or o⁡(1)o(1) worst-case error for parity, [12]’s result implies 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-completeness by reducing from exact nekomata.

We also consider average-case regimes in Table 1, which are more natural from a Fourier-analytic standpoint. Average-case performance is measured by correlation with the target function on a uniformly random input. For PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n}, average-case error can be converted to worst-case error by mapping the input to a random string of the same parity, a transformation implementable in both 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} [32] and 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0}22 2 provided access to random bits.. Analogous to the amplification possible in 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} via MAJORITY of parallel repetition, [20] showed that 1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n)1/{\mathsf{polylog}}(n)-correlation with PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n} can be amplified to exact PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n}.

Regarding upper bounds, known capabilities of 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} have been limited. Existing constructions include regimes of parity, thresholds and symmetric functions matching 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} [27, 13]. In addition, [21] show that 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} can prepare constant-weight nn-qubit Dicke states. It is unknown whether 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} contains all decision problems in 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0}. The counterpart of this question, whether 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} contains problems outside 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} has been addressed to some degree. Earlier works, [8, 32] established relational separations between the two classes. Recently, [12] was the first to establish a worst-case decision problem separating 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} and 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0}. They showed that 𝖰𝖠𝖢0∘𝖭𝖢0\mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0}\circ{\mathsf{NC}}^{0} contains 𝖳𝖢0{\mathsf{TC}}^{0}, a strictly more powerful class than 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0}, demonstrating that even limited classical fanout (via multiple copies) significantly increases the power of 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. The one-sided error in [12]’s construction is not achievable by 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} and forms the basis for their separation.

2 Technical Overview

We provide an overview of all our proof techniques organized as follows. In Section 2.1, we describe the equivalence to QLMN and the corollary leading to point (1) of Theorem 1.3. Next, in Section 2.2 we discuss the hardness of state preparations tasks which cover points (2,3) of Theorem 1.3. Finally, in Section 2.3 we focus on MAJORITY and discuss points (4,5) as well as the upper bound in Theorem 1.4. The full proofs are split into two sections, reductions (Section 4) and upper bounds (Section 5).

2.1 Characterizing 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f} Completeness

It is possible in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} to obtain a negligible but non-zero correlation with PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n} by hard-coding the answer to a small subset of the possible inputs. It is also possible to construct a state that has non-zero but negligible amplitude on the lower-weighted nekomata branch [27]. We show that any meaningful improvement over these approximations is as hard as exact parity.

Challenges and comparison to prior work.

Existing approaches for reducing from exact PARITY to approximate parity/nekomata regimes require sufficiently strong approximations. The “classical” approach involves first mapping the input to a uniformly random string of the same parity and amplifying by taking the MAJORITY of parallel runs. Since MAJORITY𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n)\texttt{MAJORITY}_{{\mathsf{polylog}}(n)} can be computed in 𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n){\mathsf{poly}}(n) size, this applies when the correlation with PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n} is at least 1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n)1/{\mathsf{polylog}}(n) [20]. In contrast, the techniques we use to prove points (1,2,3) of Theorem 1.3 do not have classical analogues. This is because, arbitrary 1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1/{\mathsf{poly}}(n) correlations with PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n} cannot be black-box amplified in 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} since they require MAJORITYn\texttt{MAJORITY}_{n}.

Prior inherently quantum approaches work by amplifying the weight on nekomata branches, but still require sufficient weight on both branches, ⟨0n|ρ|0n⟩\braket{0^{n}|\rho|0^{n}} and ⟨1n|ρ|1n⟩\braket{1^{n}|\rho|1^{n}}. Rosenthal’s nekomata amplification [27] applies to states with most of their weight on one nekomata branch and small but non-negligible weight on the other. The amplitude amplification techniques of [12], require a total constant weight on the two branches to amplify to the “good subspace” (supported only on |0n⟩,|1n⟩\ket{0^{n}},\ket{1^{n}}) in constant depth. Consequently, these methods do not apply to the regimes we consider, where the only guarantee is non-negligible weight on two branches. This forces us to dig deeper to pinpoint the additional structure in these approximation tasks.

2.1.1 Fourier concentration to Parity

Any nn-input quantum circuit CC with a designated output register has an associated real-valued Boolean function, fC:{0,1}n→[−1,1]f_{C}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to[-1,1]. This function is obtained by standard basis measurement distribution of the output qubit, or equivalently by the expected outcome on a ZZ observable. For such functions ff and 0≤k≤n0\leq k\leq n, the weight above level kk, 𝐖≥k​[f]\mathbf{W}^{\geq k}[f] is defined as [25],

𝐖≥k​[f]:=∑S⊆[n]|S|≥kf^​(S)2.\displaystyle\mathbf{W}^{\geq k}[f]:=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq[n]\\ |S|\geq k\end{subarray}}\widehat{f}(S)^{2}. (1)

This defines the Fourier mass of a nn-input 𝖰𝖠𝖢{\mathsf{QAC}} circuit CC naturally through fC^\widehat{f_{C}}.

Thus, the non-trivial direction is to show that a 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit CC for which fCf_{C} is non-concentrated produces a 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit for exact PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n}. 2.2 Felinity as a measure of state preparation complexity

Existing notions of state approximation are insufficient to characterize states that are as hard as cat states in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. Taking fidelity for example, ⟨n|0n⟩2=1/2\braket{{}_{n}|0^{n}}^{2}=1/2, so it is not the case that all states of constant fidelity with |n⟩\ket{{}_{n}} are hard. Fidelity with cat states/nekomata is only meaningful in this context when it is bounded above 1/21/2.

Another natural notion is based on mutual information between pairs of qubits. A nekomata can be thought of as a mixture over nn perfectly correlated classical bits. Thus, both nekomatas and Cat states have mutual information 11 between every pair of the nn targets. On the other hand, there are states easily preparable in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, such as |Wn⟩\ket{W_{n}}, with pairwise mutual information 1/n1/n. For a mutual-information based state hardness metric, this suggests a high cutoff, eg Ω⁡(1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n))\Omega(1/{\mathsf{polylog}}(n)). We show that states with much smaller pairwise mutual information, such as ε​|0n⟩+ε​|1n⟩+|⟂⟩\varepsilon\ket{0^{n}}+\varepsilon\ket{1^{n}}+\ket{\perp}, and much lower fidelity with any nekomata are just as hard to construct as a nekomata in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}.

The same issues arise when using other related metrics such as trace distance, phase-dependent-fidelity [27], or interaction information. We propose a new metric to quantify the complexity of state preparation tasks, felinity, parameterized by the number of targets nn.

Definition 2.1 (Felinity of a quantum state).

For a nn-qubit state ρ\rho, the felinity of ρ\rho, ℱn(ρ)∈[0,1]\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\rho)\in[0,1] is defined as

ℱn(ρ):=2∑𝒚∈{0,1}n⟨𝒚|ρ|𝒚⟩⋅⟨𝒚|X⊗n​ρ​X⊗n|𝒚⟩\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\rho):=2\sum_{\bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\braket{\bm{y}|\rho|\bm{y}}\cdot\braket{\bm{y}|X^{\otimes n}\rho X^{\otimes n}|\bm{y}}

Felinity has several natural properties, such as monotonicity, for any qubit qq of ρ\rho,

ℱn(ρ)≤ℱn−1(trqρ),\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\rho)\leq\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n-1}}(\tr_{q}\rho), (4)

and Lipschitz continuity (Lemma 4.3),

|ℱn(ρ)−ℱn(σ)|≤8TD(ρ,σ).\displaystyle|\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\rho)-\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\sigma)|\leq 8\,\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma). (5)

Felinity behaves as expected on the states discussed so far,

2.2.1 Dicke states imply parity

To demonstrate an application of felinity, we show that high-weight Dicke states can be turned into high-felinity states through a single layer of 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} gates. When discussing Dicke states, |Dkn⟩\ket{D^{n}_{k}}, we without loss of generality consider the case when the weight k≤n/2k\leq n/2. This is because any |Dn−kn⟩\ket{D^{n}_{n-k}} can be obtained by negating the bits of |Dkn⟩\ket{D^{n}_{k}}. This allows us to quantify the hardness of Dicke states as a function of kk, and the 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}-complete states as those with k=nδk=n^{\delta} for any constant δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1). Then, we state the full version of point (3) of Theorem 1.3 below.

{restatable*}

[Dicke states imply Fanout]theoremdicketocat Suppose there exists a depth dd 𝖰𝖠𝖢{\mathsf{QAC}} circuit CC using mm ancillas that, for some k≤n/2k\leq n/2, constructs a nn-qubit state ρ\rho satisfying,

TD⁡(ρ,|Dkn⟩)≤180​k,\mathrm{TD}\left(\rho,\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\right)\leq\frac{1}{80k},

Then, there is a depth d′=O⁡(d)d^{\prime}=O(d), m′=m⋅𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)m^{\prime}=m\cdot{\mathsf{poly}}(n)-ancilla 𝖰𝖠𝖢{\mathsf{QAC}} circuit C′C^{\prime} that implements FANOUTk\texttt{FANOUT}_{k}. Additionally, for δ=log⁡k/log⁡n\delta=\log k/\log n, there is a depth-O⁡(d′/δ)O(d^{\prime}/\delta), O⁡(m′​n1−δ)O(m^{\prime}n^{1-\delta}) ancillae 𝖰𝖠𝖢{\mathsf{QAC}} circuit for FANOUTn\texttt{FANOUT}_{n}.

To prove Section 2.2.1, the reduction of Section 2.1.1, which only uses classical gates does not suffice. Our key observation here is that |Dkn⟩\ket{D^{n}_{k}} has non-negligible overlap with the states |p⟩⊗n\ket{p}^{\otimes n} and (Z​|p⟩)⊗n(Z\ket{p})^{\otimes n}, for p=k/np=k/n. Although |p⟩\ket{p} and Z​|p⟩Z\ket{p} are far from orthogonal, for t≫n/kt\gg n/k, |p⟩⊗t\ket{p}^{\otimes t} and (Z​|p⟩)⊗t(Z\ket{p})^{\otimes t}, have negligible overlap. Then, we show that |Dkn⟩\ket{D^{n}_{k}} can be transformed into a state ρ\rho with non-negligible ℱℓ(ρ)\mathcal{F}_{{}_{\ell}}(\rho), by applying a layer of ℓ≈k/log⁡k\ell\approx k/\log k reflection gates, each acting as a controlled-not onto a fresh ancilla, with controls on |ρ⟩⊗t\ket{\rho}^{\otimes t}. This reduces us to Section 2.2. Then, when k=𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)k={\mathsf{poly}}(n), δ\delta is a constant, implying the following.

{restatable*}

Contrary to the equivalence between cat states and nekomatas, this reduction does not apply to an entangled version of a Dicke state, i.e a uniform mixture over strings of hamming weight kk, rather than a superposition. Perhaps a more appropriate analogue of such a state is the “Poor-man’s cat state” which is a mixture over strings of odd parity and can be prepared in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, and in fact in 𝖰𝖭𝖢0{\mathsf{QNC}}^{0} [32]. As expected, the poor man’s cat state has negl⁡(n)\mathrm{negl}(n) felinity. The state |n⟩\ket{{}_{n}} on the other hand, is a superposition over even parity strings (in the Hadamard basis), which is crucial to making its felinity 11.

In conclusion, felinity provides a concrete characterization of states that are hard to construct in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} and may be of interest to subsequent work on understanding the power of 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} through the ancilla-only state synthesis setting.

2.3 Hardness classification of Majority regimes

MAJORITY is the canonical example used to illustrate the insufficiency of Fourier concentration lower bounds for 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0}. In contrast, we show the feasible regimes of approximate MAJORITY in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} are fully determined by their Fourier concentration. First we obtain the following two corollaries as a consequence of Theorem 1.1, that show the remaining two points (4,5) of Theorem 1.3. {restatable*}[High correlation with MAJORITY implies FANOUT]corollaryhardmajority If there is a depth dd, mm-ancilla 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} whose output achieves at least (1−1nδ)(1-\frac{1}{n^{\delta}})-correlation with MAJORITYn\texttt{MAJORITY}_{n} for any constant δ>0\delta>0, then, there exists a depth d′=O⁡(d)d^{\prime}=O(d), m′=𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(m+n)m^{\prime}={\mathsf{poly}}(m+n)-ancilla circuit that exactly implements FANOUTn\texttt{FANOUT}_{n}.

Then, the result follows directly from Corollary 4.2. Next, since a worst case error of up to 1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1/{\mathsf{poly}}(n) for any function can be boosted to arbitrary (1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n))(1-1/{\mathsf{poly}}(n))-correlation through parallel repetitions, we also have the following.

{restatable*}

Then, PARITYn∈𝖰𝖠𝖢0\texttt{PARITY}_{n}\in\mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0}.

As a consequence, if MAJORITYn∈𝖡𝖰𝖠𝖢0\texttt{MAJORITY}_{n}\in\mathsf{BQAC}^{0}, i.e, can be computed with worst case error 1/31/3, then, 𝖰𝖠𝖢0=𝖰𝖠𝖢f0\mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0}=\mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0}_{f}.

Analogous 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} lower bounds to both these corollaries follow from [22]. However, much stronger 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} lower bounds for MAJORITY hold and are obtained from other techniques [26, 28]. We demonstrate next that these stronger bounds and techniques do not apply to 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}.

2.3.1 Average case quantum advantage.

We show that 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuits can achieve (1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n))(1-1/{\mathsf{polylog}}(n))-correlation with MAJORITY on average. Classically, any randomized 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} circuit can be de-randomized while preserving its average case correlation [5]. However, randomness in quantum algorithms cannot be distilled in this manner and crucially, for inputs 𝒙{\bm{x}} whose hamming weight is far from n/2n/2, the output of our circuit is not deterministic.

[12] showed that the state |Wn⟩\ket{W_{n}} can be constructed in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. We observe that any superposition of the states |0n⟩\ket{0^{n}} and |Wn⟩\ket{W_{n}} can be constructed in 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0}. Furthermore, we can implement the map |0⟩↦|0n⟩\ket{0}\mapsto\ket{0^{n}} and |1⟩↦|Wn⟩\ket{1}\mapsto\ket{W_{n}} in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} (Lemma 5.2). This allows us to implement the following map in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, which serves as a “weak fanout” gadget.

|0⟩x​|0n⟩↦|0⟩x​|0n⟩,|1⟩x​|0n⟩↦|1⟩x​|1/n⟩⊗n.\ket{0}_{x}\ket{0^{n}}\mapsto\ket{0}_{x}\ket{0^{n}},\quad\ket{1}_{x}\ket{0^{n}}\mapsto\ket{1}_{x}\ket{1/n}^{\otimes n}.

A uniformly random input has its hamming weight reasonably concentrated about n/2n/2. Thus, at a high level our strategy is to approximate MAJORITY well on these strings. 3 Preliminaries

A depth-dd 𝖰𝖠𝖢\mathsf{QAC} circuit on nn input qubits and mm ancilla qubits initialized to |0m⟩\ket{0^{m}} consists of dd layers of multi-qubit gates, in which each qubit participates in at most one gate, and arbitrary single-qubit unitaries taken to be free. We adopt the formulation of [27], where each multi-qubit gate is a reflection about a product state. Formally, a gate G⁡(S)G(S) on subset SS of qubits has the form G⁡(S)=(I−2​|θ→⟩​⟨θ→|S)G(S)=(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}) for some product state |θ→⟩S\ket{\vec{\theta}}_{S}. The single qubit unitaries are arbitrary and do not contribute to the depth. This is equivalent to [23]’s original definition where each multi-qubit gate is a Toffoli gate [27].

In most prior works on 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, the output of a circuit on input 𝒙{\bm{x}} is given by the probability of measuring |1⟩\ket{1} on a designed register tt. We consider an equivalent observables-based definition, which is more natural in the context of boolean analysis.

Definition 3.1 (Single output circuit).

Let CC be a nn-input 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit acting on mm ancillae, with a designated target register tt. The output of CC on input 𝐱∈{0,1}n{\bm{x}}\in\{0,1\}^{n} is a randomized variable ∈{±1}\in\{\pm 1\}, given by the outcome of measuring the observable Zt⊗IZ_{t}\otimes I on C​|𝐱⟩​|0m⟩C\ket{{\bm{x}}}\ket{0^{m}}. The associated real-valued boolean function computed by CC, fC:{0,1}n→{±1}f_{C}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{\pm 1\}, describes the expected output on input 𝐱{\bm{x}},

fC​(𝒙):=⟨𝒙,0m|C†⋅Zt⊗I⋅C|𝒙,0m⟩f_{C}({\bm{x}}):=\braket{{\bm{x}},0^{m}|C^{\dagger}\cdot Z_{t}\otimes I\cdot C|{\bm{x}},0^{m}}

We also consider 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} state preparation circuits that do not act on any input qubits—instead starting with |0m⟩\ket{0^{m}} on all registers. In this case, the parameter nn refers to the number of qubits in the target state and mm is required to be 𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n){\mathsf{poly}}(n).

Definition 3.2 (State preparation circuit).

A circuit CC prepares an nn-qubit state |ψ⟩X\ket{\psi}_{X} using mm qubits if,

C​|0m⟩=|ψ⟩X​|φ⟩C\ket{0^{m}}=\ket{\psi}_{X}\ket{\varphi}

for some state |φ⟩\ket{\varphi}, unentangled with |ψ⟩X\ket{\psi}_{X} on the remaining qubits. Furthermore CC cleanly prepares |ψ⟩X\ket{\psi}_{X} if |φ⟩=|0m−n⟩\ket{\varphi}=\ket{0^{m-n}}.

All our state construction upper bounds are clean preparations. When proving reductions, we don’t enforce clean preparations.

3.1 Notation

We use contractions such as ⟨ν|T\bra{\nu}_{T} on states acting on larger sub-systems, |ψ⟩T,A\ket{\psi}_{T,A}. The notation ⟨ν|T⋅|ψ⟩T,A\bra{\nu}_{T}\cdot\ket{\psi}_{T,A} refers to the un-normalized vector obtained by tracing out the TT sub-system in |ν⟩​⟨ν|T⊗IA⋅|ψ⟩\outerproduct*{\nu}{\nu}_{T}\otimes I_{A}\cdot\ket{\psi}. We also use the shorthand ⟨ψ|⋅M⋅|ψ⟩\bra{\psi}\cdot M\cdot\ket{\psi} for the operator given by (⟨ψ|⊗I)​M​(|ψ⟩⊗I)(\bra{\psi}\otimes I)M(\ket{\psi}\otimes I) when it is clear that the matrix MM acts on space larger than |ψ⟩\ket{\psi}. Then, Definition 3.1 can be rewritten, fC​(𝒙):=⟨𝒙,0m|C†​Zt​C|𝒙,0m⟩f_{C}({\bm{x}}):=\braket{{\bm{x}},0^{m}|C^{\dagger}Z_{t}C|{\bm{x}},0^{m}}

For 0≤ε≤10\leq\varepsilon\leq 1, we define |ε⟩\ket{\varepsilon} to be the single-qubit state given by |ε⟩=ε​|1⟩+1−ε​|0⟩\ket{\varepsilon}=\sqrt{\varepsilon}\ket{1}+\sqrt{1-\varepsilon}\ket{0}. This is consistent with the usual definitions of |0⟩,|1⟩\ket{0},\ket{1}. For 0≤γ≤10\leq\gamma\leq 1, define Rotγ\mathrm{Rot}_{\gamma} to be the single-qubit unitary

Rotγ:=[γ1−γ1−γ−γ].\displaystyle\mathrm{Rot}_{\gamma}:=\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{\gamma}&\sqrt{1-\gamma}\\ \sqrt{1-\gamma}&-\sqrt{\gamma}\end{bmatrix}. (10)

3.1.1 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-completeness

𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f} can be equivalently defined as the quantum analog of 𝖳𝖢0{\mathsf{TC}}^{0}, consisting of 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} and arbitrary THRESHOLDkn{}^{n}_{k} gates, i.e, 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0=QTC0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}=\textsf{QTC}^{0} [19, 13, 12]. The notion of 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-completeness can be viewed as the quantum analog of 𝖳𝖢0{\mathsf{TC}}^{0}-completeness [1]. Augmenting 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} gates with a gate for any 𝖳𝖢0{\mathsf{TC}}^{0}-complete problem provides the ability to implement any other problem in 𝖳𝖢0{\mathsf{TC}}^{0}. Canonical 𝖳𝖢0{\mathsf{TC}}^{0}-complete problems (under 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} reductions) consist of sorting, integer division and iterated multiplication [9, 18], but notably do not include PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n} (𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0}[2]⊊[2]\subsetneq 𝖳𝖢0{\mathsf{TC}}^{0}) [26, 28]. On the other hand, 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete problems (under 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} reductions) include PARITY, MAJORITY and state synthesis of any nekomata (uniform mixture of |0n⟩\ket{0^{n}} and |1n⟩\ket{1^{n}}) [23, 27, 13].

3.2 Analysis of boolean functions

In boolean analysis it is convenient to have f⁡(𝒙)∈{±1}f({\bm{x}})\in\{\pm 1\}. To accommodate standard basis inputs of the form |𝒙⟩\ket{{\bm{x}}} where 𝒙∈{0,1}n{\bm{x}}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, we define boolean functions such as PARITY, MAJORITY as {0,1}n→{±1}\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{\pm 1\} instead of {±1}n→{±1}\{\pm 1\}^{n}\to\{\pm 1\}. For a string 𝒙∈{0,1}n{\bm{x}}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, we use |𝒙|\left\lvert{\bm{x}}\right\rvert to denote the hamming weight of 𝒙{\bm{x}}. Then, PARITYn​(𝒙):=(−1)|𝒙|\texttt{PARITY}_{n}({\bm{x}}):=(-1)^{|{\bm{x}}|} and we use the following convention for MAJORITY,

MAJORITYn​(𝒙):={1if ​|𝒙|≤n/2,−1if ​|𝒙|>n/2.\texttt{MAJORITY}_{n}({\bm{x}}):=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }|{\bm{x}}|\leq n/2,\\ -1&\text{if }|{\bm{x}}|>n/2.\end{cases}

A powerful technique for analyzing boolean functions is their Fourier decomposition, for a reference we point the reader to [25]. The characters χS:{0,1}n→ℝ\chi_{S}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\mathbb{R} defined by χS(x):=(−1)⊕i∈Sxi\chi_{S}(x):=(-1)^{\oplus_{i\in S}x_{i}} form an orthonormal basis for the vector space of real-valued boolean functions. Projecting ff onto this basis reveals the Fourier decomposition of ff,

f⁡(x)=∑S⊆[n]f^​(S)​χS​(x).f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\hat{f}(S)\chi_{S}(x). (11)

By Parseval’s, ∑S⊆[n]f^​(S)2=1\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\hat{f}(S)^{2}=1. The correlation of real valued boolean functions is defined by:

Definition 3.3 (Correlation of real valued boolean functions ).

The correlation of two boolean functions f,g:{0,1}n→[−1,1]f,g:\{0,1\}^{n}\to[-1,1] is defined as,

corr⁡(f,g):=𝐄𝐱∼{0,1}nf​(𝐱)​g​(𝐱).\mathrm{corr}(f,g):=\Ex_{{\bm{x}}\sim\{0,1\}^{n}}f({\bm{x}})g({\bm{x}}).

By Parseval’s again, corr⁡(f,g)=∑S⊆[n]f^​(S)⋅g^​(S)\mathrm{corr}(f,g)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\widehat{f}(S)\cdot\widehat{g}(S). Recall the real-valued boolean function fC:{0,1}n→[−1,1]f_{C}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to[-1,1] associated with the output of CC, from Definition 3.1.

Definition 3.4 (𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit correlation with boolean function).

Given a circuit CC on nn input qubits and mm ancilla AA, with a designated output register tt, the correlation of CC with a boolean function g⁡(𝐱):{0,1}n→{±1}g({\bm{x}}):\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{\pm 1\}, corr⁡(C,g)\mathrm{corr}(C,g) is defined to the correlation between fCf_{C} and gg, given by,

corr⁡(fC,g)\displaystyle\mathrm{corr}(f_{C},g) :=𝖤𝒙∼{0,1}n​fC​(𝒙)​g​(𝒙)\displaystyle:={\mathsf{E}}_{{\bm{x}}\sim\{0,1\}^{n}}f_{C}({\bm{x}})g({\bm{x}})
=𝖤𝒙∼{0,1}n​⟨𝒙,0m|C†​Zt​C|𝒙,0m⟩​g​(𝒙)\displaystyle={\mathsf{E}}_{{\bm{x}}\sim\{0,1\}^{n}}\braket{{\bm{x}},0^{m}|C^{\dagger}Z_{t}C|{\bm{x}},0^{m}}g({\bm{x}})

3.3 Procedures in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}

Note the following form of the standard un-computing ancillae technique for quantum circuits due to [6]. We include a proof of this specific formulation in Appendix A.

Claim 3.5 (Approximate clean computation [6]).

Let CC be a nn-input depth dd single-output 𝖰𝖠𝖢{\mathsf{QAC}} circuit using mm ancillae such that, on input 𝐱∈{0,1}n{\bm{x}}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, the output register measures to |0⟩\ket{0} with probability p0​(𝐱)p_{0}({\bm{x}}) and 11 with probability p1​(𝐱)=1−p0​(𝐱)p_{1}({\bm{x}})=1-p_{0}({\bm{x}}). Then there exists a nn-input 𝖰𝖠𝖢{\mathsf{QAC}} circuit C′C^{\prime} of depth O⁡(d)O(d) with m′=m+n+1m^{\prime}=m+n+1 ancillae such that for all 𝐱{\bm{x}}, conditioning on the non-output registers being clean produces the (unnormalized) vector,

⟨0m′−1|A⋅C′​(𝒙)​|𝒙⟩​|0m′⟩A,t=p0​(𝒙)​|𝒙⟩​|0⟩t+p1​(𝒙)​|𝒙⟩​|1⟩t\bra{0^{m^{\prime}-1}}_{A}\cdot C^{\prime}({\bm{x}})\ket{{\bm{x}}}\ket{0^{m^{\prime}}}_{A,t}=p_{0}({\bm{x}})\ket{{\bm{x}}}\ket{0}_{t}+p_{1}({\bm{x}})\ket{{\bm{x}}}\ket{1}_{t}

In other words, C′⋅|𝐱⟩​|0m′⟩C^{\prime}\cdot\ket{{\bm{x}}}\ket{0^{m^{\prime}}} has amplitude exactly pb​(𝐱)p_{b}({\bm{x}}) on |𝐱⟩​|b⟩​|0m′−1⟩\ket{{\bm{x}}}\ket{b}\ket{0^{m^{\prime}-1}}, and all the non-output registers are returned to their starting state with probability p0​(𝐱)2+p1​(𝐱)2p_{0}({\bm{x}})^{2}+p_{1}({\bm{x}})^{2}.

We will also need the following primitives.

Fact 3.6.

Let 𝖱|ψ⟩:=I−2​|ψ⟩⟨ψ|{\mathsf{R}}_{\ket{\psi}}:=I-2\outerproduct{\psi}{\psi}. If state |ψ⟩​|0n⟩\ket{\psi}\ket{0^{n}} can be constructed by a 𝖰𝖠𝖢0​(d,s){\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}(d,s) circuit acting on |0m⟩\ket{0^{m}}, then 𝖱|ψ⟩{\mathsf{R}}_{\ket{\psi}} can be implemented by a depth 2​d+12d+1 𝖰𝖠𝖢0​(2​d+1,2​s+1){\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}(2d+1,2s+1) circuit with the same number of ancillae.

For any k=𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n)k={\mathsf{polylog}}(n),

[13] also showed that the exact amplitude amplification technique of [15, 7] can be performed in 𝖰𝖠𝖢{\mathsf{QAC}}. We will use the following sub-routines that are equivalent in the single-round special case.

Fact 3.8 (Claim 2.4 of [20]).

Suppose there exists a depth-dd mm-qubit 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit to construct |ψ⟩T,A=C​|0m⟩\ket{\psi}_{T,A}=C\ket{0^{m}} satisfying,

Claim 3.9.

Let |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} be any nn qubit state. Suppose there exists a depth-dd mm-ancilla 𝖰𝖠𝖢{\mathsf{QAC}} circuit CC that cleanly prepares the following n+1n+1-qubit state |φ⟩\ket{\varphi},

Let γ:=1/(2​α)\gamma:=1/(2\alpha), and let 𝖼​-​𝖱γ\mathsf{c}\text{-}{\mathsf{R}}_{\gamma} denote the controlled 𝖱γ{\mathsf{R}}_{\gamma} gate. Using a fresh ancilla aa, we can prepare the following state cleanly in depth d+1d+1,

|ψ0⟩\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{0}} :=𝖼​-​𝖱γ​(t,a)⋅|φ⟩T,t​|0⟩a\displaystyle:=\mathsf{c}\text{-}{\mathsf{R}}_{\gamma}(t,a)\cdot\ket{\varphi}_{T,t}\ket{0}_{a} (12)
=α​|ψ⟩T​|1⟩a​𝖱γ​|0⟩t+1−α​|bad⟩T​|0⟩a​|0⟩t\displaystyle=\sqrt{\alpha}\ket{\psi}_{T}\ket{1}_{a}{\mathsf{R}}_{\gamma}\ket{0}_{t}+\sqrt{1-\alpha}\ket{\mathrm{bad}}_{T}\ket{0}_{a}\ket{0}_{t} (13)
=1/2​|ψ⟩T​|1⟩a​|1⟩t+3/2​|bad′⟩T,t​|0⟩a\displaystyle=1/2\ket{\psi}_{T}\ket{1}_{a}\ket{1}_{t}+\sqrt{3}/2\ket{\mathrm{bad}^{\prime}}_{T,t}\ket{0}_{a} (14)

Applying a ZZ gate on aa, we obtain,

|ψ1⟩\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{1}} :=−1/2|ψ⟩T|1⟩a|1⟩t+3/2|bad′⟩T,t|0⟩a.\displaystyle:=-1/2\ket{\psi}_{T}\ket{1}_{a}\ket{1}_{t}+\sqrt{3}/2\ket{\mathrm{bad}^{\prime}}_{T,t}\ket{0}_{a}. (15)

Then, applying 𝖱|ψ0⟩{\mathsf{R}}_{\ket{\psi_{0}}} which can be implemented in depth 2​d+12d+1 by Fact 3.6, we obtain

=|ψ⟩​|1⟩t,a.\displaystyle=\ket{\psi}\ket{1}_{t,a}. (17)

Finally to clean up, we can apply XX gates to t,at,a without increasing depth. ∎

To prove the equivalence between Conjecture 1 and PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n}, we will first reduce PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n} to the following weak-nekomata state which we show is 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete.

Lemma 4.1 (Skewed nekomata to exact parity).

Let CC be a depth-dd 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit acting on mm qubits that constructs the state |ψ⟩T,A=C​|0m⟩\ket{\psi}_{T,A}=C\ket{0^{m}} satisfying ‖|0n⟩​⟨0n|T⋅|ψ⟩‖2≥1/4\left\lVert\outerproduct*{0^n}{0^n}_{T}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2}\geq 1/4 and ‖|1n⟩​⟨1n|T⋅|ψ⟩‖2≥ε\left\lVert\outerproduct*{1^n}{1^n}_{T}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2}\geq\varepsilon for some non-negligible ε\varepsilon. Then, there exists a depth d′=O⁡(d)d^{\prime}=O(d) circuit that, using m′=m⋅𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)m^{\prime}=m\cdot{\mathsf{poly}}(n) ancillae prepares an exact nekomata state.

Proof.

WLOG, for a real and non-negative γ≥1/2\gamma\geq 1/2 the state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} can be written as

|ψ⟩\displaystyle\ket{\psi} =γ​|0n⟩T​|α0⟩A+ε​|1n⟩T​|α1⟩A+1−γ−ε​|⟂⟩T,A.\displaystyle=\sqrt{\gamma}\ket{0^{n}}_{T}\ket{\alpha_{0}}_{A}+\sqrt{\varepsilon}\ket{1^{n}}_{T}\ket{\alpha_{1}}_{A}+\sqrt{1-\gamma-\varepsilon}\ket{\perp}_{T,A}. (38)

Now, using a fresh ancilla aa and two gates controlled on |0n⟩\ket{0^{n}} and |1n⟩\ket{1^{n}} to mark the nekomata branches, we obtain

|ψ1⟩\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{1}} =(I−2​|0n⟩​⟨0n|⊗|+⟩⟨+|a)⋅(I−2​|1n⟩​⟨1n|⊗|+⟩⟨+|a)⋅|ψ⟩​|0⟩a\displaystyle=(I-2\outerproduct*{0^n}{0^n}\otimes\outerproduct*{+}{+}_{a})\cdot(I-2\outerproduct*{1^n}{1^n}\otimes\outerproduct*{+}{+}_{a})\cdot\ket{\psi}\ket{0}_{a} (39)
=γ​|0n⟩T​|α0⟩A​|1⟩a+ε​|1n⟩T​|α1⟩A​|1⟩a+1−γ−ε​|⟂⟩T,A​|0⟩a.\displaystyle=\sqrt{\gamma}\ket{0^{n}}_{T}\ket{\alpha_{0}}_{A}\ket{1}_{a}+\sqrt{\varepsilon}\ket{1^{n}}_{T}\ket{\alpha_{1}}_{A}\ket{1}_{a}+\sqrt{1-\gamma-\varepsilon}\ket{\perp}_{T,A}\ket{0}_{a}. (40)

Then we apply Claim 3.9 to amplify the “good” amplitude and discard the cleaned up aa register to produce the state

|ψ1⟩\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{1}} =1−ε1​|0n⟩T​|α0⟩A+ε1​|1n⟩T​|α1⟩A.\displaystyle=\sqrt{1-\varepsilon_{1}}\ket{0^{n}}_{T}\ket{\alpha_{0}}_{A}+\sqrt{\varepsilon_{1}}\ket{1^{n}}_{T}\ket{\alpha_{1}}_{A}. (41)

where ε1=ε/γ≥ε\varepsilon_{1}=\varepsilon/\gamma\geq\varepsilon is still non-negligible.

Next observe that the parallel amplification technique of [27] can now be used to obtain a high fidelity nekomata using m1:=Θ⁡(1/ε12)m_{1}:=\Theta(1/\varepsilon_{1}^{2}) copies and one layer. Imagine arranging these copies into a grid, each copy in a row. Then for each column i∈[n]i\in[n], apply an OR of all qubits with output unto a fresh register qiq_{i}. The registers Q={q1​…​qn}Q=\left\{q_{1}\dots q_{n}\right\} now make up the new nekomata targets. To see this, the probability of this measuring to all 00 is

‖⟨0n|Q⋅|ψ⟩‖2\displaystyle\left\lVert\bra{0^{n}}_{Q}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2} =(1−ε1)2​m1≈1/e.\displaystyle=\left(\sqrt{1-\varepsilon_{1}}\right)^{2m_{1}}\approx 1/e. (42)

The remaining probability is all 11s. This produces a high-fidelity approximation of a nekomata, allowing us to apply Fact 3.8 to obtain an exact nekomata and thus FANOUTn\texttt{FANOUT}_{n} or PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n}. ∎

We now show that a generalized “threshold-block” nekomata is 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete.

\twobranchdicke
Proof.

Let DD be the distribution over {0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n} supported on strings of Hamming weight at least kk given by the squared amplitudes of Π≥kn​|ψ⟩‖Π≥kn⋅|ψ⟩‖\frac{\Pi^{n}_{\geq k}\ket{\psi}}{\left\lVert\Pi^{n}_{\geq k}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert} in standard basis. Then we will show there exist ℓ=Θ⁡(klog2​k)\ell=\Theta\!\left(\frac{k}{\log^{2}k}\right) disjoint nonempty subsets S1,…,Sℓ⊆[n]S_{1},\dots,S_{\ell}\subseteq[n] such that

Pr𝒙∼D[∀j∈[ℓ],𝒙|Sj≢0]≥c\displaystyle\Pr_{{\bm{x}}\sim D}\!\left[\forall j\in[\ell],\;{\bm{x}}|_{S_{j}}\not\equiv 0\right]\geq c (43)

for some absolute constant c>0c>0. Let ℓ=⌊klog2​k⌋.\ell=\left\lfloor\frac{k}{\log^{2}k}\right\rfloor. Partition [n][n] uniformly at random into ℓ\ell nonempty disjoint sets S1,…,SℓS_{1},\dots,S_{\ell} of (almost) equal size. Then for every jj,

|Sj|≥n2​ℓ.\displaystyle|S_{j}|\geq\frac{n}{2\ell}. (44)

Note the standard bound for any t≥kt\geq k,

(n−|Sj|t)(nt)≤(1−|Sj|n)t≤e−t|Sj|/n≤e−k/(2ℓ)=e−Θ⁡(log2​k).\frac{\binom{n-|S_{j}|}{t}}{\binom{n}{t}}\leq\left(1-\frac{|S_{j}|}{n}\right)^{t}\leq e^{-t|S_{j}|/n}\leq e^{-k/(2\ell)}=e^{-\Theta(\log^{2}k)}.

Fix any x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{n} with Hamming weight t≥kt\geq k, and let T=supp⁡(x)T=\mathrm{supp}(x). For a fixed jj,

Pr[T∩Sj=∅]\displaystyle\Pr[T\cap S_{j}=\varnothing] =(n−|Sj|t)(nt)≤e−Θ⁡(log2​k).\displaystyle=\frac{\binom{n-|S_{j}|}{t}}{\binom{n}{t}}\leq e^{-\Theta(\log^{2}k)}. (45)

By a union bound over all ℓ\ell blocks,

Pr[∃j:T∩Sj=∅]≤ℓ⋅e−Θ⁡(log2​k).\displaystyle\Pr[\exists j:T\cap S_{j}=\varnothing\big]\leq\ell\cdot e^{-\Theta(\log^{2}k)}. (46)

Since ℓ≤k\ell\leq k, the right-hand side is o⁡(1)o(1), and in particular for large enough kk,

Pr[∀j,T∩Sj≠∅]≥910.\Pr[\forall j,\;T\cap S_{j}\neq\varnothing\big]\geq\frac{9}{10}. (47)

Thus, for a random partition, every fixed xx of weight at least kk hits all ℓ\ell blocks with Ω⁡(1)\Omega(1) probability. Averaging over x∼Dx\sim D implies that there exists a fixed choice of S1,…,SℓS_{1},\dots,S_{\ell} achieving the desired bound.

Apply an 𝙾𝚁\mathtt{OR} gate for each of these subsets onto a fresh ancilla. Then, Lemma 4.1 completes the reduction. ∎

Using this reduction, we can now prove the equivalence between PARITY and QLMN.

4.1 Parity equivalence of Quantum LMN

Corollary 4.2 (High Degree Fourier mass to PARITY computation).

Suppose there exists a depth dd, mm-ancilla single-output 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit CC acting on nn inputs, such that for some k≥nδk\geq n^{\delta},

𝐖≥k​[fC]≥ε,\mathbf{W}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]\geq\varepsilon,

then, there exists a depth O⁡(d)O(d), O⁡((m+n)⋅log2⁡(k)/ε)O((m+n)\cdot\log^{2}(k)/\varepsilon)-ancilla 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit C′C^{\prime} for PARITYk\texttt{PARITY}_{k} and a depth O⁡(d/δ),O~​((m+n)⋅n1−δ/ε)O(d/\delta),\tilde{O}((m+n)\cdot n^{1-\delta}/\varepsilon)-ancilla 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit for PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n}.

Proof.

By Section 2.1.1 we can construct a 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit C′C^{\prime} that prepares a state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} satisfying ‖⟨0n|⋅|ψ⟩‖2≥1/2\left\lVert\bra{0^{n}}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2}\geq 1/2 and ‖Π≥kn⋅|ψ⟩‖2≥ε/2\left\lVert\Pi^{n}_{\geq k}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2}\geq\varepsilon/2. Therefore, if ε\varepsilon is non-negligible, Section 2.1.1 implies a 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit for for PARITYk/log2​k\texttt{PARITY}_{k/\log^{2}k} with O⁡(d)O(d) depth, and O⁡((m+n)/ε)O((m+n)/\varepsilon) ancilla. By the classical divide and conquer argument, there exists a O⁡(d)O(d) depth, O⁡((m+n)​log2⁡(n)/ε)O((m+n)\log^{2}(n)/\varepsilon) ancilla 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit for PARITYk\texttt{PARITY}_{k}, and a circuit for PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n} with a O⁡(1/δ)O(1/\delta) multiplicative blowup in depth and n1−δn^{1-\delta} blowup in ancillae. ∎

We now have all the pieces to complete the proof of Theorem 1.1. See 1.1

Proof.

Therefore sW≥k​[f𝒞]>Θ~​(S⁡(Θ⁡(d),k))\frac{s}{W^{\geq k}[f_{\mathcal{C}}]}>\tilde{\Theta}(S(\Theta(d),k)) (as clearly S⁡(d,k)≥kS(d,k)\geq k), and hence s⋅Θ~​(S⁡(Θ⁡(d),k))−1>W≥k​[f𝒞]s\cdot\tilde{\Theta}\left(S(\Theta(d),k)\right)^{-1}>W^{\geq k}[f_{\mathcal{C}}], which implies QLMN​(Θ~​(S​(Θ​(d),k)))\text{QLMN}\left(\tilde{\Theta}\left(S(\Theta(d),k)\right)\right). 4.1.1 Consequences for 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete problems

We now present some consequences of the equivalence of QLMN and PARITY∉𝖰𝖠𝖢0\texttt{PARITY}\not\in{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} for 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete problems. 4.2 Felinity and 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete states

Recall the notion of Felinity, restated below. See 2.1 We will first show the two main properties of felinity that will be used in subsequent reductions. These are: (1) felinity behaves naturally under trace distance (Lemma 4.3) (2) a circuit for preparing an nn-qubit ρ\rho produces a circuit for ℱn(ρ)\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\rho) correlation with parity PARITYn\texttt{PARITY}_{n} (Section 2.2).

Lemma 4.3 (Felinity is Lipschitz-continuous).

Let ρ,σ\rho,\sigma be nn-qubit states. Then

|ℱn(ρ)−ℱn(σ)|≤8TD(ρ,σ),|\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\rho)-\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\sigma)|\leq 8\,\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma),

where TD⁡(ρ,σ):=12​‖ρ−σ‖1.\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma):=\frac{1}{2}\|\rho-\sigma\|_{1}.

Proof.

Consider the computational basis measurement on 2​n2n-qubit states. For any 𝒚,𝒛∈{0,1}n\bm{y},\bm{z}\in\{0,1\}^{n} and a nn-qubit state ρ′\rho^{\prime}, define,

qρ′​(𝒚​𝒛)\displaystyle q_{\rho^{\prime}}(\bm{y}\bm{z}) :=⟨𝒚,𝒛|ρ′⊗ρ′|𝒚,𝒛⟩=⟨𝒚|ρ′|𝒚⟩​⟨𝒛|ρ′|𝒛⟩\displaystyle:=\braket{\bm{y},\bm{z}|\rho^{\prime}\otimes\rho^{\prime}|\bm{y},\bm{z}}=\braket{\bm{y}|\rho^{\prime}|\bm{y}}\braket{\bm{z}|\rho^{\prime}|\bm{z}} (56)

This is precisely the probability of the measurement outcome 𝒚​𝒛∈{0,1}2​n\bm{y}\bm{z}\in\{0,1\}^{2n} on the 2​n2n-qubit state ρ′⊗ρ′\rho^{\prime}\otimes\rho^{\prime}. From triangle inequality and contractivity of trace distance under measurement,

12​∑𝒚,𝒛∈{0,1}n|qρ​(𝒚​𝒛)−qσ​(𝒚​𝒛)|\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\bm{y},\bm{z}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\left\lvert q_{\rho}(\bm{y}\bm{z})-q_{\sigma}(\bm{y}\bm{z})\right\rvert ≤TD⁡(ρ⊗ρ,σ⊗σ)\displaystyle\leq\mathrm{TD}(\rho\otimes\rho,\sigma\otimes\sigma) (57)
≤2​T​D​(ρ,σ).\displaystyle\leq 2\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma). (58)

For 𝒚∈{0,1}n\bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, let 𝒚¯\overline{\bm{y}} be the string obtained by flipping all bits of 𝒚\bm{y}, i.e, |𝒚¯⟩=X⊗n​|𝒚⟩\ket{\overline{\bm{y}}}=X^{\otimes n}\ket{\bm{y}}. Then,

|ℱn(ρ)−ℱn(σ)|\displaystyle\left\lvert\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\rho)-\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\sigma)\right\rvert =2​|∑𝒚∈{0,1}nqρ​(𝒚​𝒚¯)−qσ​(𝒚​𝒚¯)|\displaystyle=2\left\lvert\sum_{\bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}q_{\rho}(\bm{y}\overline{\bm{y}})-q_{\sigma}(\bm{y}\overline{\bm{y}})\right\rvert (59)
≤2​∑𝒚∈{0,1}n|qρ​(𝒚​𝒚¯)−qσ​(𝒚​𝒚¯)|\displaystyle\leq 2\sum_{\bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\left\lvert q_{\rho}(\bm{y}\overline{\bm{y}})-q_{\sigma}(\bm{y}\overline{\bm{y}})\right\rvert (60)
≤2​∑𝒚,𝒛∈{0,1}n|qρ​(𝒚​𝒛)−qσ​(𝒚​𝒛)|\displaystyle\leq 2\sum_{\bm{y},\bm{z}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\left\lvert q_{\rho}(\bm{y}\bm{z})-q_{\sigma}(\bm{y}\bm{z})\right\rvert (61)
≤8​T​D​(ρ,σ).\displaystyle\leq 8\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma). (62)

∎

Recall that we treat the output of the circuit as as a ±1\pm 1 valued measurement outcome. Any Hermitian matrix 𝒪\mathcal{O} is a valid observable corresponding to a measurement with possible outcomes among the eigenvalues of 𝒪\mathcal{O}. For a state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi}, the expected outcome of measuring 𝒪\mathcal{O} on |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} is given by ⟨ψ|𝒪|ψ⟩\braket{\psi|\mathcal{O}|\psi}. For nn-input, mm-ancillae 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit CC with a designated target tt, define the following observable,

𝒪C:=⟨0→m|A⋅C†​Zt​C⋅|0→m⟩A\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{C}:=\bra{{\vec{0}}^{m}}_{A}\cdot{C^{\dagger}Z_{t}C}\cdot\ket{{\vec{0}}^{m}}_{A} (63)

Physically, 𝒪C\mathcal{O}_{C} can be interpreted as the Heisenberg evolution of the output measurement. Mathematically, 𝒪C\mathcal{O}_{C} is simply a 2n×2n2^{n}\times 2^{n} Hermitian matrix with eigenvalues in [−1,1][-1,1] satisfying fC​(𝒙)=⟨𝒙|𝒪C|𝒙⟩f_{C}({\bm{x}})=\braket{{\bm{x}}|\mathcal{O}_{C}|{\bm{x}}}. With this formalism in mind, we proceed to show the main property of felinity.

G\displaystyle G :=(I−|0m⟩​⟨0m|)A⊗Ia+|0m⟩​⟨0m|A⊗Xa\displaystyle:=(I-\outerproduct*{0^m}{0^m})_{A}\otimes I_{a}+\outerproduct*{0^m}{0^m}_{A}\otimes X_{a} (64)
=I−2​|0m⟩​⟨0m|A⊗|−⟩⟨−|a\displaystyle=I-2\outerproduct*{0^m}{0^m}_{A}\otimes\outerproduct*{-}{-}_{a} (65)

C′:=G​C†​L​C\displaystyle C^{\prime}:=GC^{\dagger}LC (66)

and is a depth 2​d+22d+2 circuit with m+1m+1 ancillae.

First define the observable 𝒪C′\mathcal{O}_{C^{\prime}} corresponding to measurement outcome of C′C^{\prime}, s.t fC′=⟨𝒙|𝒪C′|𝒙⟩f_{C^{\prime}}=\braket{{\bm{x}}|\mathcal{O}_{C^{\prime}}|{\bm{x}}}

𝒪C′\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{C^{\prime}} =⟨0Am,0a|(C′)†​Za⊗IA​C′|0Am,0a⟩\displaystyle=\braket{0^{m}_{A},0_{a}|(C^{\prime})^{\dagger}Z_{a}\otimes I_{A}C^{\prime}|0^{m}_{A},0_{a}} (67)
=⟨0Am,0a|C†​L​C​G†​Za​G​C†​L​C|0Am,0a⟩\displaystyle=\braket{0^{m}_{A},0_{a}|C^{\dagger}LCG^{\dagger}Z_{a}GC^{\dagger}LC|0^{m}_{A},0_{a}} (L=L†)\displaystyle\qquad(L=L^{\dagger}) (68)
=⟨ψA,0a|L​C​G†​Za​G​C†​L|ψA,0a⟩\displaystyle=\braket{\psi_{A},0_{a}|LCG^{\dagger}Z_{a}GC^{\dagger}L|\psi_{A},0_{a}} (69)
=⟨ψ|A⋅L​C​⟨0a|G†​Za​G|0a⟩​C†​L†⋅|ψ⟩A\displaystyle=\bra{\psi}_{A}\cdot LC\braket{0_{a}|G^{\dagger}Z_{a}G|0_{a}}C^{\dagger}L^{\dagger}\cdot\ket{\psi}_{A} (70)

4.2.1 Poly weight Dicke states are 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete

It is known that any Dicke state |Dnk⟩\ket{D^{k}_{n}} can be constructed in 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}, i.e using FANOUTn\texttt{FANOUT}_{n}. We will show that constructing |Dnk⟩\ket{D^{k}_{n}} in constant depth requires FANOUTmin⁡(k,n−k)\texttt{FANOUT}_{\min(k,n-k)}.

Definition 4.4 (Uniform kk-hamming slice / Dicke 𝒟kn\mathcal{D}^{n}_{k}).

The uniform distribution on all nn-bit strings of hamming weight kk. The associated state is |Dkn⟩\ket{D^{n}_{k}}, the nn-qubit kk-weight Dicke state,

|Dkn⟩:=(nk)−1/2∑b∈{0,1}n,|b|=k|b⟩.\ket{D^{n}_{k}}:=\binom{n}{k}^{-1/2}\sum_{b\in\{0,1\}^{n},|b|=k}\ket{b}.

We will focus on k≤n/2k\leq n/2 WLOG, since |Dnn−k⟩\ket{D^{n-k}_{n}} has the same complexity as |Dkn⟩\ket{D^{n}_{k}}.

Fact 4.5 (Binomial distribution bounds [14]).

For any sufficiently large n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, and any k≤n/2k\leq n/2

Pr[𝖡𝗂𝗇𝗈𝗆(n,k/n)=k]≥e−1k\Pr[\mathsf{Binom}(n,k/n)=k]\geq\frac{e^{-1}}{\sqrt{k}}

To prove 𝖰𝖠𝖢f0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-completeness of Dicke state preparation, we first prove the following reduction from Dicke states to non-negligible felinity states.

Lemma 4.6.

For any nn and k≤n/2k\leq n/2, there is a single layer LL of 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} gates acting on n+ℓn+\ell qubits for ℓ=⌊k/log⁡k⌋\ell=\lfloor k/\log k\rfloor, such that, the state |ψ⟩=L​|Dkn⟩​|0ℓ⟩T\ket{\psi}=L\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\ket{0^{\ell}}_{T} satisfies,

ℱℓ(trT¯|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|)≥18​k.\mathcal{F}_{{}_{\ell}}\left(\tr_{\overline{T}}\outerproduct*{\psi}{\psi}\right)\geq\frac{1}{8k}.
Proof.

Partition the qubits into ℓ=⌊k/log⁡k⌋\ell=\lfloor k/\log k\rfloor blocks. Let BiB_{i} be the mi=|Bi|≥n/ℓm_{i}=|B_{i}|\geq n/\ell qubits in each block, and label a corresponding qubit of TT as tit_{i}. Let p=knp=\frac{k}{n}. Then, LL is given by,

L\displaystyle L =⨂i∈[ℓ](IBi−|p⟩​⟨p|⊗mi⊗|+⟩⟨+|ti)\displaystyle=\bigotimes_{i\in[\ell]}(I_{B_{i}}-\outerproduct*{p}{p}^{\otimes m_{i}}\otimes\outerproduct*{+}{+}_{t_{i}}) (89)
=⨂i∈[ℓ][(IBi−|p⟩​⟨p|⊗mi)⊗Iti+|p⟩​⟨p|⊗mi⊗Xti].\displaystyle=\bigotimes_{i\in[\ell]}\left[(I_{B_{i}}-\outerproduct*{p}{p}^{\otimes m_{i}})\otimes I_{t_{i}}+\outerproduct*{p}{p}^{\otimes m_{i}}\otimes X_{t_{i}}\right]. (90)

As described in Eq. 90, each gate can be viewed as a controlled-not gate, that flips tit_{i} whenever BiB_{i} lies in the |p⟩​⟨p|⊗mi\outerproduct*{p}{p}^{\otimes m_{i}} subspace. Now, for |ψ⟩=L​|Dkn⟩​|0ℓ⟩\ket{\psi}=L\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\ket{0^{\ell}}, we will first argue that ‖⟨1ℓ|T⋅|ψ⟩‖2≥ε\left\lVert\bra{1^{\ell}}_{T}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2}\geq\varepsilon and ‖⟨0ℓ|T⋅|ψ⟩‖2≥ε\left\lVert\bra{0^{\ell}}_{T}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2}\geq\varepsilon. From Eq. 90, we have,

‖⟨1ℓ|T⋅|ψ⟩‖2\displaystyle\left\lVert\bra{1^{\ell}}_{T}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2} =‖⟨p|⊗n⋅|ψ⟩‖2\displaystyle=\left\lVert\bra{p}^{\otimes n}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2} (91)
=‖⟨p|⊗n⋅|Dkn⟩‖2\displaystyle=\left\lVert\bra{p}^{\otimes n}\cdot\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\right\rVert^{2} (92)
=Pr[𝖡𝗂𝗇𝗈𝗆(n,p)=k]\displaystyle=\Pr\left[\mathsf{Binom}(n,p)=k\right] (93)
≥e−1k.(from Fact 4.5)\displaystyle\geq\frac{e^{-1}}{\sqrt{k}}.\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\text{(from \lx@cref{creftype~refnum}{fact:binombounds})} (94)

similarly, letting Π=⨂i∈[ℓ](I−|p⟩​⟨p|⊗mi)\Pi=\bigotimes_{i\in[\ell]}(I-\outerproduct*{p}{p}^{\otimes m_{i}}),

‖⟨0ℓ|T⋅|ψ⟩‖2\displaystyle\left\lVert\bra{0^{\ell}}_{T}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2} =‖Π⋅|Dkn⟩‖2.\displaystyle=\left\lVert\Pi\cdot\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\right\rVert^{2}. (95)

Instead of directly bounding ‖Π​|Dkn⟩‖2\left\lVert\Pi\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\right\rVert^{2}, we bound |⟨ν|Dkn⟩|2\left\lvert\braket{\nu|D^{n}_{k}}\right\rvert^{2} for a vector |ν⟩\ket{\nu} that is nearly a +1+1 eigenvector of Π\Pi. Define, |p−⟩=1−p​|0⟩−p​|1⟩\ket{p_{-}}=\sqrt{1-p}\ket{0}-\sqrt{p}\ket{1}.

Observe that, for each ii,

⟨p−|p⟩2​mi\displaystyle\braket{p_{-}|p}^{2m_{i}} =(1−2​p)2​mi\displaystyle=(1-2p)^{2m_{i}} (96)
≤exp(−4k/ℓ)\displaystyle\leq\exp(-4k/\ell) (97)
=1k4.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{k^{4}}. (98)

Therefore,

‖Π​|p−⟩⊗n‖2\displaystyle\left\lVert\Pi\ket{p_{-}}^{\otimes n}\right\rVert^{2} =∏i∈[ℓ](1−|⟨p|p−⟩|2​mi)\displaystyle=\prod_{i\in[\ell]}(1-\left\lvert\braket{p|p_{-}}\right\rvert^{2m_{i}}) (99)
≥(1−1/k4)ℓ\displaystyle\geq\left(1-1/k^{4}\right)^{\ell} (100)
≥1−1/k3.\displaystyle\geq 1-1/k^{3}. (101)

Therefore, |p−⟩⊗n\ket{p_{-}}^{\otimes n} is nearly an eigenvector of Π\Pi, and,

‖Π⋅|Dkn⟩‖\displaystyle\left\lVert\Pi\cdot\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\right\rVert ≥|⟨p−|⊗n⋅|Dkn⟩|−1/k3/2\displaystyle\geq\left\lvert\bra{p_{-}}^{\otimes n}\cdot\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\right\rvert-1/k^{3/2} (102)
=‖⟨p|⊗n⋅Z⊗n​|Dkn⟩‖−1/k3/2\displaystyle=\left\lVert\bra{p}^{\otimes n}\cdot Z^{\otimes n}\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\right\rVert-1/k^{3/2} (103)
=‖(−1)k⋅⟨p|⊗n​|Dkn⟩‖−1/k3/2\displaystyle=\left\lVert(-1)^{k}\cdot\bra{p}^{\otimes n}\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\right\rVert-1/k^{3/2} (104)
=Pr[𝖡𝗂𝗇𝗈𝗆(n,p)=k]−1/k3/2\displaystyle=\sqrt{\Pr\left[\mathsf{Binom}(n,p)=k\right]}-1/k^{3/2} (105)
≥e−1.01k1/4.\displaystyle\geq\frac{e^{-1.01}}{k^{1/4}}. (106)

Hence, ‖Π⋅|Dkn⟩‖2≳1/k\left\lVert\Pi\cdot\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\right\rVert^{2}\gtrsim 1/\sqrt{k}.

Combining with Eq. 95 and Eq. 94, for ρT=trT¯​|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|\rho_{T}=\tr_{\overline{T}}\outerproduct*{\psi}{\psi},

ℱℓ(ρT)\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{{}_{\ell}}(\rho_{T}) ≥⟨0ℓ|ρT|0ℓ⟩​⟨1ℓ|ρT|1ℓ⟩\displaystyle\geq\braket{0^{\ell}|\rho_{T}|0^{\ell}}\braket{1^{\ell}|\rho_{T}|1^{\ell}} (107)
≥18​k.(using e2.01≈7.5)\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{8k}.\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\text{(using $e^{2.01}\approx 7.5$)} (108)

∎

TD⁡(σ,σ∗)\displaystyle\mathrm{TD}(\sigma,\sigma^{*}) ≤TD⁡(ρ⊗|0ℓ⟩​⟨0ℓ|,|Dkn⟩​|0ℓ⟩)\displaystyle\leq\mathrm{TD}(\rho\otimes\outerproduct*{0^{\ell}}{0^{\ell}},\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\ket{0^{\ell}}) (109)

By Section 2.2, this implies a depth O⁡(d)O(d), m⋅𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)m\cdot{\mathsf{poly}}(n)-ancilla circuit for FANOUTℓ\texttt{FANOUT}_{\ell}. Note log⁡ℓ/log⁡k=1−o⁡(1)\log\ell/\log k=1-o(1). Then, using the recursive nature of FANOUT [23, 27], this provides a depth d′=O⁡(d)d^{\prime}=O(d), m′=m⋅𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)m^{\prime}=m\cdot{\mathsf{poly}}(n)-ancilla circuit for FANOUTk\texttt{FANOUT}_{k}, as well as a depth O⁡(d′/δ)O(d^{\prime}/\delta), O⁡(m′​n1−δ)O(m^{\prime}n^{1-\delta}) ancillae circuit for FANOUTn\texttt{FANOUT}_{n}. ∎

5 Upper bounds for 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}

We now prove some important building blocks for our construction of a circuit with high MAJORITY correlation. We will first show that “poor-man’s fanout” lies in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, and then combine this with a “weak-copy” test, which estimates the hamming weight of the original string these weak copies were made from.

The “poor-mans fanout” circuit is an upgraded version of a controlled-WW map, which we use in its implementation.

Claim 5.1 (Uniform 0n0^{n} and WnW_{n}).

For any nn, the state |Wn′⟩=12​|0n⟩+12​|Wn⟩\ket{W^{\prime}_{n}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{0^{n}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{W_{n}} can be cleanly prepared in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} using O⁡(n)O(n) qubits.

Proof.

Start with the state |ψ0⟩T:=|1/p⟩⊗n\ket{\psi_{0}}_{T}:=\ket{1/p}^{\otimes n} for p=1/(n+1)p=1/(n+1). Observe that,

p1:=Prx∼𝖡𝖾𝗋𝗇⁡(1/n+1,n)[|x|=1]\displaystyle p_{1}:=\Pr_{x\sim\mathsf{Bern}(1/{n+1},n)}\left[|x|=1\right] =n⋅(p)⋅(1−p)n\displaystyle=n\cdot(p)\cdot(1-p)^{n} (114)
=(1−p)n\displaystyle=(1-p)^{n} (115)
=Prx∼𝖡𝖾𝗋𝗇⁡(1/n+1,n)[|x|=0].\displaystyle=\Pr_{x\sim\mathsf{Bern}(1/{n+1},n)}\left[|x|=0\right]. (116)

Then, applying the THRESHOLD1n\texttt{THRESHOLD}^{n}_{1}, which is in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, onto a new ancilla aa, we can prepare,

|ψ1⟩T,a\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{1}}_{T,a} =THRESHOLD1n​|ψ0⟩T​|0⟩a\displaystyle=\texttt{THRESHOLD}^{n}_{1}\ket{\psi_{0}}_{T}\ket{0}_{a} (117)
=p1​|Wn′⟩T​|1⟩a+1−p1​|bad⟩T​|0⟩a.\displaystyle=\sqrt{p_{1}}\ket{W^{\prime}_{n}}_{T}\ket{1}_{a}+\sqrt{1-p_{1}}\ket{\mathrm{bad}}_{T}\ket{0}_{a}. (118)

From known binomial bounds (see Fact 4.5), limn→∞p1=e−1≈0.367\lim_{n\to\infty}p_{1}=e^{-1}\approx 0.367. Hence p1≥1/4p_{1}\geq 1/4 and applying Claim 3.9 produces |Wn′⟩\ket{W^{\prime}_{n}} cleanly. ∎

Lemma 5.2 (Controlled W map).

We can apply the following map cleanly in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}:

|0⟩x​|0n⟩↦|0⟩x​|0n⟩,|1⟩x​|0n⟩↦|1⟩x​|Wn⟩.\ket{0}_{x}\ket{0^{n}}\mapsto\ket{0}_{x}\ket{0^{n}},\quad\ket{1}_{x}\ket{0^{n}}\mapsto\ket{1}_{x}\ket{W_{n}}.
Proof.

One can construct the following state using an 𝙾𝚁\mathtt{OR} gate, then an additional X​ZXZ gate on qubit xx from Claim 5.1.

|φ⟩=12​|1⟩x​|0n⟩−12​|0⟩x​|Wn⟩.\displaystyle\ket{\varphi}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{1}_{x}\ket{0^{n}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{0}_{x}\ket{W_{n}}. (119)

We can implement 𝖱φ=(I−2​|φ⟩​⟨φ|){\mathsf{R}}_{\varphi}=(I-2\outerproduct*{\varphi}{\varphi}), the reflection about this state in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} using Fact 3.6. This has the effect of swapping the two branches. Then, on input b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\}, first construct the state, using Claim 5.1.

|ψ0​(b)⟩\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{0}(b)} :=|b⟩x​|Wn′⟩\displaystyle:=\ket{b}_{x}\ket{W^{\prime}_{n}} (120)
=12​|b⟩x​|0n⟩+12​|b⟩x​|Wn⟩\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{b}_{x}\ket{0^{n}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{b}_{x}\ket{W_{n}} (121)

Next, apply 𝖱φ{\mathsf{R}}_{\varphi} to obtain |ψ1​(b)⟩\ket{\psi_{1}(b)}. Observe that when b=1b=1, we have,

|ψ1​(1)⟩\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{1}(1)} :=𝖱φ​|ψ0​(1)⟩\displaystyle:={\mathsf{R}}_{\varphi}\ket{\psi_{0}(1)} (122)
=12​(𝖱φ​|1⟩x​|0n⟩)+12​|1⟩x​|Wn⟩\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left({\mathsf{R}}_{\varphi}\ket{1}_{x}\ket{0^{n}}\right)+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{1}_{x}\ket{W_{n}} (123)
=12​|0⟩x​|Wn⟩+12​|1⟩x​|Wn⟩\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{0}_{x}\ket{W_{n}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{1}_{x}\ket{W_{n}} (124)
=|+⟩x​|Wn⟩\displaystyle=\ket{+}_{x}\ket{W_{n}} (125)

Because the |1⟩​|Wn⟩\ket{1}\ket{W_{n}} branch is orthogonal to |φ⟩\ket{\varphi}. Similarly, when b=0b=0, we obtain the state |ψ1​(0)⟩=|+⟩x​|0n⟩\ket{\psi_{1}(0)}=\ket{+}_{x}\ket{0^{n}}. To make this map clean, we can apply an HH gate on xx and then another 𝙾𝚁\mathtt{OR} gate to recover the input value of bb. ∎

Corollary 5.3 (Any superposition of |0n⟩\ket{0^{n}}, |Wn⟩\ket{W_{n}}).

For any α,β\alpha,\beta such that |α|2+|β|2=1\left\lvert\alpha\right\rvert^{2}+\left\lvert\beta\right\rvert^{2}=1, we can prepare the state, |Wn​(α,β)⟩:=α​|0n⟩+β​|Wn⟩\ket{W_{n}(\alpha,\beta)}:=\alpha\ket{0^{n}}+\beta\ket{W_{n}} in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}.

Proof.

To prepare the desired superposition, start with a qubit |ν⟩x=α​|0⟩+β​|1⟩\ket{\nu}_{x}=\alpha\ket{0}+\beta\ket{1} and apply the circuit from Lemma 5.2. To uncompute qubit xx apply an 𝙾𝚁\mathtt{OR} gate. ∎

5.2 Majority

For ease of description we will use the following claim formally connecting classical post-processing with limited fanout to 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuits.

Claim 5.5 (Closure under 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} postprocessing).

Let UU be a 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit that, on input 𝐱{\bm{x}}, produces output qubits whose computational-basis measurement outcomes form a distribution 𝒟⁡(𝐱)\mathcal{D}({\bm{x}}) over {0,1}m⁡(n)\{0,1\}^{m(n)}. Suppose there is an 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} circuit TT with 𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n){\mathsf{polylog}}(n) fanout satisfying, for all 𝐱∈{0,1}n{\bm{x}}\in\{0,1\}^{n},

Pr𝒚∼𝒟⁡(𝒙)[T(𝒚))=g(𝒙)]≥1−δ\Pr_{\bm{y}\sim\mathcal{D}({\bm{x}})}[T(\bm{y}))=g({\bm{x}})]\geq 1-\delta

for a function g⁡(𝐱)g({\bm{x}}), then there is a 𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(m){\mathsf{poly}}(m) size single-output 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit CC (Definition 3.1) such that,

corr⁡(fC,g)≥1−2​δ.\mathrm{corr}(f_{C},g)\geq 1-2\delta.
Proof.

Using Fact 3.7, there is a 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit C′C^{\prime} acting on mm inputs that, using 𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(m){\mathsf{poly}}(m) ancillae, implements the following map for all 𝒚∈{0,1}m\bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{m},

|𝒚⟩X​|0⟩t↦|𝒚⟩X​|T⁡(𝒚)⟩t\displaystyle\ket{\bm{y}}_{X}\ket{0}_{t}\mapsto\ket{\bm{y}}_{X}\ket{T(\bm{y})}_{t} (137)

Now, observe that any measurement on the XX register in the output does not affect measurements on the tt register (since they commute). Prepend UU to C′C^{\prime}, so that the mm output qubits of UU, feed into the inputs of C′C^{\prime} to obtain CC that acts on nn inputs.

Then, on any input 𝒙∈{0,1}n{\bm{x}}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, apply CC and measure both tt and XX in the standard basis. The distribution on tt is exactly the one obtained by applying T⁡(𝒚)T(\bm{y}) on a sample from 𝒟⁡(𝒙)\mathcal{D}({\bm{x}}). Thus the resulting circuit outputs g⁡(𝒙)g({\bm{x}}) with probability at least 1−δ⁡(n)1-\delta(n) on every input, which corresponds to correlation 1−2​δ​(n)1-2\delta(n) with g⁡(𝒙)g({\bm{x}}). ∎

Poor man’s fanout allows us to create nn “weaker” copies of the input. In order to approximate majority, we can separately apply 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuits to each copy to estimate majority and amplify. A gadget with similar properties to poor man’s fanout was given in Appendix B of [12]. The lemma below, which will serve as the key ingredient in our test, is analogous to their Claim 28.

Lemma 5.6 (𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit for APPROXt\texttt{APPROX}_{t}).

Let a=𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n)a={\mathsf{polylog}}(n) and let t∈{0,…,n}t\in\{0,\dots,n\}. 23λt(ℓ−tn)2≤Pr[Z=1]≤43λt(ℓ−tn)2.\frac{2}{3}\lambda_{t}\left(\frac{\ell-t}{n}\right)^{2}\leq\Pr[Z=1]\leq\frac{4}{3}\lambda_{t}\left(\frac{\ell-t}{n}\right)^{2}.

Using 𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n){\mathsf{polylog}}(n) fanout, make ss copies of the input string 𝒙{\bm{x}}. For each copied string and each i∈[n]i\in[n], apply Section 2.3.1 to the copied bit xix_{i}. For each u∈[n]u\in[n], the uuth fanout outputs across i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n form one copy of the encoded input |x1/n⟩⋯|xn/n⟩\ket{x_{1}/n}\cdots\ket{x_{n}/n}. Thus we obtain s​n≥r​msn\geq rm unentangled encoded inputs, and hence r​mrm independent copies Zj,kZ_{j,k} of ZZ, with j∈[m]j\in[m] and k∈[r]k\in[r].

Let Wj=⋁k=1rZj,kW_{j}=\bigvee_{k=1}^{r}Z_{j,k}. In the first case, Pr[Wj=1]≤rPr[Z=1]≤2/3\Pr[W_{j}=1]\leq r\Pr[Z=1]\leq 2/3. In the second,

Pr[Wj=1]=1−(1−Pr[Z=1])r≥1−(1−2​λt3​n​a2)r≥1−e−2.\Pr[W_{j}=1]=1-(1-\Pr[Z=1])^{r}\geq 1-\left(1-\frac{2\lambda_{t}}{3na^{2}}\right)^{r}\geq 1-e^{-2}.

By a well-known result of Ajtai and Ben-Or [2], there is an approximate-majority function on mm bits, that is, a function Am:{0,1}m→{0,1}A_{m}:\{0,1\}^{m}\to\{0,1\} computable by an 𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{AC}}^{0} circuit of size 𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(m){\mathsf{poly}}(m), which outputs 11 whenever the input Hamming weight is below 0.7​m0.7m and outputs 00 whenever it is above 0.8​m0.8m. Since m=O⁡(log⁡n)m=O(\log n), this circuit has size, and hence fanout, at most 𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n){\mathsf{polylog}}(n). Applying AmA_{m} to W1,…,WmW_{1},\dots,W_{m} therefore gives the desired output with probability at least 1−1/n1-1/n, and the result follows from Claim 5.5. ∎

\ezmajority
Proof.

Let γ=na\gamma=\frac{\sqrt{n}}{a} and η=n2​a\eta=\frac{\sqrt{n}}{2a}. For each threshold tt, let DtD_{t} be the 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit from Lemma 5.6 . Thus, on inputs of Hamming weight ℓ\ell, DtD_{t} outputs 11 with probability at least 1−1/n1-1/n if |ℓ−t|<η|\ell-t|<\eta, and outputs 00 with probability at least 1−1/n1-1/n if |ℓ−t|>γ|\ell-t|>\gamma.

Let L=c′​log⁡(n)​nL=c^{\prime}\log{n}\sqrt{n} for a sufficiently large constant c′c^{\prime}, and consider thresholds

T+={n/2+j​η:1≤j≤L/η},T−={n/2−j​η:1≤j≤L/η}.T_{+}=\{n/2+j\eta:1\leq j\leq L/\eta\},\qquad T_{-}=\{n/2-j\eta:1\leq j\leq L/\eta\}.

Since |T+∪T−|=𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n)|T_{+}\cup T_{-}|={\mathsf{polylog}}(n), we may run all the circuits DtD_{t} in parallel. Let CC output 11 if some DtD_{t} with t∈T+t\in T_{+} outputs 11, output 00 if some DtD_{t} with t∈T−t\in T_{-} outputs 11, and output an arbitrary bit otherwise. By Claim 5.5, this is computable in 𝖰𝖠𝖢0{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}.

If γ<ℓ−n/2≤L\gamma<\ell-n/2\leq L, then some t∈T+t\in T_{+} satisfies |ℓ−t|<η|\ell-t|<\eta, while every t∈T−t\in T_{-} satisfies |ℓ−t|>γ|\ell-t|>\gamma. Hence, except with probability at most |T+∪T−|/n|T_{+}\cup T_{-}|/n, the circuit CC outputs 1=MAJORITYn​(x)1=\texttt{MAJORITY}_{n}(x). The case −L≤ℓ−n/2<−γ-L\leq\ell-n/2<-\gamma is symmetric.

Thus CC can disagree with MAJORITYn\texttt{MAJORITY}_{n} only if one of the above tests outputs the wrong answer, if |ℓ−n/2|≤γ|\ell-n/2|\leq\gamma, or if |ℓ−n/2|>L|\ell-n/2|>L. The first case contributes at most |T+∪T−|/n=𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n)/n|T_{+}\cup T_{-}|/n={\mathsf{polylog}}(n)/n failure probability. To analyze the second case, for a uniformly random input, the probability that the hamming weight ℓ\ell satisfies |ℓ−n/2|≤γ|\ell-n/2|\leq\gamma is at most O⁡(γ/n)=O⁡(1/a)O(\gamma/\sqrt{n})=O(1/a). For the last case, the probability that ℓ\ell satisfies |ℓ−n/2|>L|\ell-n/2|>L is at most 2e−2L2/n=O(1/n)2e^{-2L^{2}/n}=O(1/n). Each of these contributions is O⁡(1/a)O(1/a). Therefore CC agrees with MAJORITYn\texttt{MAJORITY}_{n} on a 1−O⁡(1/a)1-O(1/a) fraction of inputs, and hence has correlation at least 1−1/a1-1/a after adjusting constants. ∎

Lemma A.1 (Felinity of uniformly rotated W states).

For any state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} of the form |ψ⟩:=U⊗n​|Wn⟩\ket{\psi}:=U^{\otimes n}\ket{W_{n}} for any unitary UU,

ℱn(ψ)=negl(n).\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\psi)=\mathrm{negl}(n).
Proof.

UU can be written in its Euler angle decomposition as,

U=ei​δ​Rz​(α)​Ry​(β)​Rz​(γ).\displaystyle U=e^{i\delta}R_{z}(\alpha)R_{y}(\beta)R_{z}(\gamma). (160)

Observe that any global phases and any matrices that commute with ZZ do not affect the felinity, since it is defined with respect to ZZ-basis measurements. Therefore, all the RzR_{z} rotations commute and it suffices to analyze Ry​(β)R_{y}(\beta), i.e, the state |φ⟩:=Ry​(β)⊗n​|Wn⟩\ket{\varphi}:=R_{y}(\beta)^{\otimes n}\ket{W_{n}}.

|φ⟩\ket{\varphi} lies in the symmetric subspace, and we can express it in the Dicke basis:

|φ⟩=∑k=0nαk​|Dkn⟩,\displaystyle\ket{\varphi}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\alpha_{k}\ket{D_{k}^{n}}, (161)

Then,

ℱn(φ)\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\varphi) =2⋅∑k=0n(nk)−1⋅|αk|2⋅|αn−k|2\displaystyle=2\cdot\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}^{-1}\cdot\left\lvert\alpha_{k}\right\rvert^{2}\cdot\left\lvert\alpha_{n-k}\right\rvert^{2} (162)

Identify the symmetric subspace with the spin-j=n/2j=n/2 irreducible representation of S​U​(2)SU(2), under which |Dkn⟩\ket{D_{k}^{n}} corresponds to the angular momentum eigenstate |j=n/2,m=k−n/2⟩\ket{j=n/2,\,m=k-n/2}. Thus,

αk\displaystyle\alpha_{k} =⟨Dkn|​Ry​(β)⊗n​|D1n⟩\displaystyle=\bra{D_{k}^{n}}R_{y}(\beta)^{\otimes n}\ket{D_{1}^{n}} (163)
=dk−n/2, 1−n/2n/2​(β),\displaystyle=d^{\,n/2}_{\,k-n/2,\;1-n/2}(\beta), (164)

where dm′,mj​(β)d^{j}_{m^{\prime},m}(\beta) denotes the Wigner small-dd matrix. We require the entry for m′=k−n/2m^{\prime}=k-n/2 and m=1−n/2m=1-n/2. These matrix elements are well known and admit explicit closed-form expression. For e.g., see section (4.3.4) of [31] which provides the entry we need in terms of Jacobi polynomials. From this, one obtains,

|αk|≤𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)⋅(nk)⋅cosn−k−1⁡(β2)​sink−1⁡(β2)\displaystyle\left\lvert\alpha_{k}\right\rvert\leq{\mathsf{poly}}(n)\cdot\sqrt{\binom{n}{k}}\cdot\cos^{n-k-1}\left(\frac{\beta}{2}\right)\sin^{k-1}\left(\frac{\beta}{2}\right) (165)

Then, since sin2​θ​cos2​θ\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta is at most 1/41/4, each term of the summation in Eq. 162 can be bounded by,

(nk)−1​|αk|2​|αn−k|2\displaystyle\binom{n}{k}^{-1}|\alpha_{k}|^{2}|\alpha_{n-k}|^{2} ≤𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)​(sin⁡(β/2)⋅cos⁡(β/2))2​n−4\displaystyle\leq{\mathsf{poly}}(n)\left(\sin(\beta/2)\cdot\cos(\beta/2)\right)^{2n-4} (166)
≤𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)​(1/2)2​n−4\displaystyle\leq{\mathsf{poly}}(n)(1/2)^{2n-4} (167)
=negl⁡(n)\displaystyle=\mathrm{negl}(n) (168)

Therefore,

ℱn(ψ)=ℱn(φ)=negl(n)\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\psi)=\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\varphi)=\mathrm{negl}(n) (169)
